title: Sandboxed Code Execution Service
summary: Compile and run untrusted code submissions safely against test suites during live contests.
statement:
Design the execution backend for a coding assessment and competition platform where users submit source code in languages like Java, Python, C++, and Rust and receive verdicts (`Accepted`, `Wrong Answer`, `Time Limit Exceeded`, `Memory Limit Exceeded`, `Runtime Error`).

Functional requirements:
- Users run code interactively against sample inputs and submit solutions evaluated against 50 to 200 hidden test cases.
- Enforce strict per-problem CPU time and memory limits.
- Submitted code is completely untrusted and must never access the network, host data, other users' submissions, or hidden test answers.
- Return test verdicts within a few seconds during normal load and degrade gracefully during scheduled weekly contests.

Scale to assume:
- 2 million daily submissions on average.
- Scheduled contests spike to 60,000 submissions per minute at contest start and close.
- Each submission runs for up to 5 seconds of CPU time and 512 MB of memory.
hints: Compute how many worker CPU cores you need during a 60,000-submissions-per-minute contest spike, and why the HTTP API cannot hold a synchronous request open while running 100 test cases.
Running untrusted C++ or Python inside a plain Docker container with default settings is unsafe and spawning a fresh VM per test case is slow. How do you get strong isolation AND fast startup?
What stops user code from fork-bombing the worker, printing 10 GB to stdout, or reading the expected-output files off disk?
expectations: Clarifies supported languages, interactive sample runs versus full contest submissions, determinism of timing, and contest fairness.
Sizes worker CPU cores from peak submissions per second multiplied by average CPU seconds per submission, motivating autoscaled warm worker pools.

Accepts submissions asynchronously (`202 Accepted`), persists source code, enqueues into priority/language queues (interactive runs prioritized over batch contest runs), and pushes status via SSE/WebSockets or polling.

Isolates untrusted code inside microVMs or hardened containers using Linux namespaces, cgroups (CPU, memory, PID caps against fork bombs), `seccomp` syscall allowlists, read-only filesystems, and zero network interfaces.
Compiles once per submission and runs the test suite inside a single sandboxed harness process (comparing outputs outside the untrusted process so user code never sees expected answers).
Maintains pre-warmed language runtime sandboxes rotated/recycled cleanly after execution, and caches immutable test-case bundles on local worker SSDs.
Caps stdout/stderr/tmpfs byte sizes, enforces both CPU-time and wall-clock timeouts, and bounds retries so deterministic crashers cannot poison workers.
